blocks.text: Κἠγὼ μὲν δώσω τᾷ παρθένῳ αὐτίκα φάσσαν, Ἐκ τᾶς ἀρκεύθῳ καθελὼν, τηνεὶ γὰρ ἐφείσδει. [Kēgō men dōsō tai parthenōi autika phassan, Ek tas arkeuthō kathelōn, tēnei gar epheisdei.] But you, my maiden, happy one, shall be given a wood pigeon, whose nest lies hidden in the lofty timber of a juniper.

But Albertus and Turner also assert that the livia dove nests in temples. And it is known from Herodotus ^{c)} what happened to Aristodicus when ἐξαῖρε τοὺς στρουθοὺς, καὶ ἄλλα ὅσα ἦν νενοσσευμένα ὀρνίθων γένεα ἐν τῷ νηῷ [exaire tous strouthous, kai alla hosa ēn nenosseumena ornithōn genea en tō nēō], he took out the sparrows and the other kinds of birds that were nesting in the temple ^{(3)}. The Hebrews, it is true, deny that any birds settled on the temple at Jerusalem, because they were driven off by what they called כולה עורב [II, 594], placed on the very top of the roof. Kimchi on Psal. LXXXIV.: בגג הבית עשו דבר שם כדי שלא ינוח שם עוף והיו קורין אותו כולה עורב, They made something on the roof of the temple so that birds should not rest there, and it was called chole oreb, that is, keeping off ravens. This is frequently mentioned in the Talmud. Thus in the tractate Middoth, ch. 4, fol. 71a, in the Gloss: וכולה עורב מאבד העורבים לפי שהיה מקיף ההיכל למעלה מן המעקה מארבע רוחותיו בחשק של ברזל גובה אמה חד כמו הסיף כדי שלו ישב עליו שום עוף על ההיכל מפני שנחתכים רגליו באותו הסיף, And the chole oreb destroyed ravens, because it surrounded the temple above the parapet on all four sides with an iron band a cubit high, sharp like a sword, so that no bird should settle on the temple, since its feet would be cut off by that sword. And in the tractate On the Sabbath, ch. 9, fol. 90a, on the word לכליא עורב (for so it reads there), the Glossator writes: טבלאת של אמה היו עושין והן חדין כסכין סביבותיה ומסמרין חדין בכלן ומחפין בהן גגו של היכל למנוע את העורבי׳ מלישב, They made plates a cubit in size, sharp all round like a knife and all furnished with sharp nails, with which they covered the roof of the temple to keep off the ravens, so that they would not settle on it. And in the tractate [col. 54] Menachoth, ch. 13, fol. 107a, the Gloss defines כולה העורב as מסמרות חדין תחובין בראש גג ההיכל לכלות העורבי׳ שלא ישבו עליו, sharp nails fixed in the top of the temple roof to prevent the ravens from sitting on it. And another Gloss in the same place: כמין טבלה חדה וקיפה על צידה וחדודה לחתוך כמו סכין, A kind of sharp plate set up on its edge, with an edge like a knife for cutting. And the Aruch: עשה צורה להבריח בה העופות מגג ההיכל כדרך שעושין עכשיו שומרי זרעים, They made a μορμολύκειον [mormolykeion], with which to chase birds from the temple roof, as those who guard crops do now. And again: במקדש ראשון ששכינה שרוייה בו לא היו צורכין כלה עורב שלא היו עופות פורחין עליו אבל במקדש שני שלו היתה קדושתו כקדושת ראשון הוצרכו לכלה עורב, Because the divine majesty dwelt in the first Sanctuary, there was no need for a προβασκανίῳ [probaskaniō]. For birds did not fly over it. But it was needed in the second, because the holiness of the second was not like that of the first. Yet something of the kind is described even in Solomon's temple by Eupolemus, when he says ^{d)} that he made δακτυλίους δύο χαλκοῦς ἀλυσιδωτοὺς, καὶ στῆσαι αὐτοὺς [daktylious dyo chalkous halysidōtous, kai stēsai autous] (read δικτύας δύο χαλκᾶς ἀλυσιδωτὰς, καὶ στῆσαι αὐτὰς [diktyas dyo chalkas halysidōtas, kai stēsai autas]) ἐπὶ μηχανημάτων ὑπερεχόντων τῷ ὕψει τὸν ναὸν πήχεις κ΄, καὶ σκιάζειν ἐπάνω παντὸς τοῦ ἱεροῦ, καὶ προσκρεμάσαι ἑκάστῃ δικτύϊ κώδωνας χαλκοῦς ταλαντιαίους τετρακοσίους, καὶ ποιῆσαι ὅλας τὰς δικτύας πρὸς τὸ ψοφεῖν τοὺς κώδωνας, καὶ ἀποσοβεῖν τὰ ὄρνεα, ὅπως μὴ καθίζῃ ἐπὶ τοῦ ἱεροῦ, μηδὲ νοσσεύῃ ἐπὶ τοῖς φατνώμασι τῶν πυλῶν, καὶ στοῶν, καὶ μολύνῃ τοῖς ἀποπατήμασι τὸ ἱερὸν [epi mēchanēmatōn hyperechontōn tō hypsei ton naon pēcheis k', kai skiazein epanō pantos tou hierou, kai proskremasai hekastē diktyi kōdōnas chalkous talantiaious tetrakosious, kai poiēsai holas tas diktyas pros to psophein tous kōdōnas, kai aposobein ta ornea, hopōs mē kathizē epi tou hierou, mēde nosseuē epi tois phatnōmasi tōn pylōn, kai stoōn, kai molynē tois apopatēmasi to hieron], two bronze nets linked with rings, and that he set them on machines which rose twenty cubits above the temple and overshadowed the whole of it, and hung from each net [II, 595] four hundred bells of great weight, and fitted all those nets so that the bells would ring and drive off the birds with their sound, so that they would not settle on the temple, nor nest in the coffered ceilings of the gates or porticoes, nor pollute the temple with their droppings. But in the first book of Kings, where Solomon's temple is accurately described, you will find nothing of the sort; nor in Josephus, although he writes the same of the temple built by Herod, On the Jewish War book 6, ch. 6: Κατὰ κορυφὴν δὲ χρυσέους ὀβελοὺς ἀνεῖχε τεθηγμένους, ὡς μή τινι προσκαθεζομένῳ μολύνοιτο τῶν ὀρνέων [Kata koryphēn de chryseous obelous aneiche tethēgmenous, hōs mē tini proskathezomenō molynoito tōn orneōn], On the top it bristled with very sharp golden spits, so that it should not be polluted by birds settling on it. This agrees well enough with the description of the כלה עורב handed down by the Talmudists. Yet suppose that Solomon's temple too bristled with such spits on the ridge of the roof: this would have kept the birds off the top, but not off the whole roof or the other parts of the temple. If Christ could stand unharmed ἐπὶ τὸ πτερύγιον τοῦ ἱεροῦ [epi to pterygion tou hierou], on the pinnacle of the temple, Matth. IV, 5., how much more little birds ^{(4)}?
